claim: miR-128 is predominantly expressed in the brains and spinal cords of E14.5 mice
source: As previously reported (Tan et al., 2013), miR-128 was found to be predominantly expressed in the brains and spinal cords of E14.5 mice, and no signal was detected with a scrambled miRNA probe (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A and references a prior publication (Tan et al., 2013)

claim: miR-128 is highly expressed in the brain and spinal cord at E17.5
source: Real-time qPCR analyses of miR-128 from various tissues at E17.5, showing that miR-128 is highly expressed in the brain and spinal cord.
evidence: qPCR data presented in Figure 1B demonstrates tissue-specific expression patterns

claim: miR-128 is expressed in cells within the ventricular/subventricular zone (VZ/SVZ) at E14.5
source: Within the E14.5 forebrain, miR-128 was clearly detectable in the cortical layers, and high-magnification images of cortical slices at E14.5 revealed the expression of miR-128 in cells within the ventricular/subventricular zone (VZ/SVZ) (Figure 1C).
evidence: In situ hybridization images in Figure 1C show miR-128 expression in specific cortical regions

claim: NPCs within the VZ/SVZ express miR-128
source: To further confirm this, we performed fluorescence ISH in combination with immunostaining using the NPC marker NESTIN in cortical slices at E14.5 and found that NPCs within the VZ/SVZ expressed miR-128 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Fluorescence ISH combined with NESTIN immunostaining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 demonstrates co-expression

claim: NPCs isolated from the E14.5 forebrain co-express miR-128 and NESTIN
source: Furthermore, NPCs isolated from the E14.5 forebrain co-expressed miR-128 and NESTIN (Figure 1D), indicating the potential functional role of miR-128 in regulating the proliferation and/or differentiation of NPCs.
evidence: Figure 1D shows co-expression data from isolated NPCs, with inference about functional role

claim: Overexpression of miR-128 results in a 15-fold upregulation of miR-128 in transfected NPCs
source: When we transfected primary embryonic NPCs that were isolated from E14.5 mouse forebrains with these constructs, the miR-128-1 precursor was efficiently processed to generate the mature miRNA, as shown by a 15-fold upregulation of miR-128 in transfected cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: qPCR quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A demonstrates the efficiency of overexpression

claim: miR-Zip-128 transfection results in efficient knockdown of endogenous miR-128
source: In addition, miR-Zip-128 transfection resulted in efficient knockdown of endogenous miR-128 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: qPCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B demonstrates knockdown efficiency

claim: Overexpression of miR-128 inhibits NPC proliferation by 56%
source: Overexpression of miR-128 inhibited NPC proliferation, as indicated by a 56% reduction in BrdU incorporation in transfected cells (arrowheads) compared with the incorporation in those transfected with the miRNA mimic control (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: BrdU incorporation assay data shown in Figure 2B and C quantifies the reduction in proliferation

claim: miR-128 knockdown leads to a 50% increase in the number of GFP-BrdU double-positive cells
source: Conversely, miR-128 knockdown led to a 50% increase in the number of GFP-BrdU double-positive cells compared to the scramble control (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: BrdU incorporation data in Figure 2D and E shows increased proliferation upon miR-128 knockdown

claim: Upregulation or downregulation of miR-128 level does not affect apoptosis in NPCs
source: These results showed that upregulation or downregulation of the miR-128 level specifically affected cell proliferation without affecting apoptosis.
evidence: TUNEL assay and cleaved caspase-3 staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 demonstrate no effect on apoptosis

claim: miR-128 overexpression increases neuronal differentiation of NPCs by approximately 100%
source: Intriguingly, miR-128 overexpression increased the neuronal differentiation of NPCs, as shown by a significant increase (of approximately 100%) in the number of GFP and TUJ1 double-positive cells (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: TUJ1 immunostaining data in Figure 2G and H quantifies the increase in neuronal differentiation

claim: miR-128 knockdown results in a 40% decrease of GFP-TUJ1 double-positive cells
source: In contrast, miR-128 knockdown resulted in a 40% decrease of GFP-TUJ1 double-positive cells compared with treatment with the scrambled control miRNA (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: TUJ1 immunostaining data in Figure 2I and J shows decreased neuronal differentiation upon miR-128 knockdown

claim: miR-128 overexpression significantly decreases the number of GFP and GFAP double-positive cells
source: To further test whether the enhanced differentiation was restricted to a neuronal fate, we immunostained NPCs with a specific antibody against GFAP, a marker for glial cells, and observed that miR-128 overexpression significantly decreased the number of GFP and GFAP double-positive cells, indicating that NPCs that had exited the cell cycle following miR-128 overexpression may have over-committed to neuronal differentiation, preventing NPCs from becoming glial cells.
evidence: GFAP immunostaining data in Figure 2—figure supplement 5 shows decreased glial differentiation, with inference about neuronal commitment

claim: miR-128 overexpression leads to a significant decrease in the percentage of horizontal divisions (10% ± SD)
source: We found a significant decrease in the percentage of horizontal divisions upon miR-128 overexpression (Figure 3A and B, 10% ± SD), while miR-128 knockdown led to a significant increase in this percentage (Figure 3A and C, 20% ± SD).
evidence: Mitotic spindle orientation analysis shown in Figure 3A and B quantifies the change in division orientation

claim: miR-128 knockdown leads to a significant increase in the percentage of horizontal divisions (20% ± SD)
source: We found a significant decrease in the percentage of horizontal divisions upon miR-128 overexpression (Figure 3A and B, 10% ± SD), while miR-128 knockdown led to a significant increase in this percentage (Figure 3A and C, 20% ± SD).
evidence: Mitotic spindle orientation analysis shown in Figure 3A and C quantifies the change in division orientation

claim: miR-128 overexpression leads to a marked decrease (~12%) in the percentage of EdU-positive cells
source: Furthermore, miR-128 overexpression led to a marked decrease in the percentage of cells that were positively labeled for the incorporation of 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU) (Ishino et al., 2014) (~12%) (Figure 3D and E), reduced cell division, as indicated by immunostaining with Ki67 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B), and a marked decrease in the number of cells that were positive for the AP marker PAX6 (28% reduction in the number of VZ/SVZ cells that were positive for both GFP and PAX6) (Figure 3H and I) and SOX2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: EdU incorporation data in Figure 3D and E, along with Ki67, PAX6, and SOX2 immunostaining, demonstrates reduced proliferation of apical progenitors

claim: miR-128 overexpression leads to a 28% reduction in the number of VZ/SVZ cells positive for both GFP and PAX6
source: Furthermore, miR-128 overexpression led to a marked decrease in the percentage of cells that were positively labeled for the incorporation of 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU) (Ishino et al., 2014) (~12%) (Figure 3D and E), reduced cell division, as indicated by immunostaining with Ki67 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B), and a marked decrease in the number of cells that were positive for the AP marker PAX6 (28% reduction in the number of VZ/SVZ cells that were positive for both GFP and PAX6) (Figure 3H and I) and SOX2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: PAX6 immunostaining data in Figure 3H and I quantifies the reduction in apical progenitors

claim: miR-128 overexpression leads to a 60% increase in the number of TBR2-positive cells
source: MiR-128 overexpression led to an increase in the number of TBR2-positive cells (60% increase in GFP-TBR2 double-positive cells) (Figure 3L and M), while miR-128 knockdown resulted in a decrease in the number of TBR2-positive cells (30% decrease in GFP-TBR2 double-positive cells) (Figure 3N and O).
evidence: TBR2 immunostaining data in Figure 3L and M quantifies the increase in basal progenitors

claim: miR-128 knockdown results in a 30% decrease in the number of TBR2-positive cells
source: MiR-128 overexpression led to an increase in the number of TBR2-positive cells (60% increase in GFP-TBR2 double-positive cells) (Figure 3L and M), while miR-128 knockdown resulted in a decrease in the number of TBR2-positive cells (30% decrease in GFP-TBR2 double-positive cells) (Figure 3N and O).
evidence: TBR2 immunostaining data in Figure 3N and O quantifies the decrease in basal progenitors

claim: miR-128 overexpression increases the number of cells positive for both GFP and EdU but negative for Ki67 by ~40%
source: Compared to the control treatment, miR-128 overexpression increased the number of cells that were positive for both GFP and EdU but negative for Ki67 cells (by ~40%), indicating an increase the number of BPs that had exited the cell cycle (Figure 3P and Q).
evidence: EdU and Ki67 double labeling data in Figure 3P and Q quantifies the increase in cell cycle exit

claim: miR-128 overexpression significantly increases the number of NEUN-positive neurons in the CP zone by ~25%
source: miR-128 overexpression significantly increased (by ~25%) the number of NEUN-positive neurons in the CP zone compared with the number in the control condition (Figure 3T and U).
evidence: NEUN immunostaining data in Figure 3T and U quantifies the increase in neurogenesis at E17.5

claim: TargetScan and miRanda identified 800 and 940 potential targets of miR-128, respectively
source: To further characterize the molecular mechanisms that underlie the changes in NPC competence, we utilized two widely used in silico microRNA target prediction algorithms (TargetScan and miRanda) (Mi et al., 2013; Witkos et al., 2011), which identified 800 and 940 potential targets of miR-128, respectively (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Bioinformatics analysis using established prediction algorithms identified potential targets, as referenced in Mi et al., 2013 and Witkos et al., 2011

claim: 77 genes were identified as overlapping targets by both TargetScan and miRanda
source: Among the 77 overlapping targets identified using two algorithms, only 53 genes were annotated to have known biological processes and thus selected for further testing (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Bioinformatics analysis identified overlapping predictions between two algorithms

claim: qPCR analysis revealed 21 genes that were downregulated upon miR-128 overexpression in cultured NPCs
source: qPCR analysis of cultured NPCs that overexpressed miR-128 revealed 21 genes that were downregulated (Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: qPCR data shown in Figure 4—source data 2 demonstrates downregulation of candidate targets

claim: Eleven genes exhibited consistent reduction in mRNA levels upon miR-128 overexpression in cultured mouse NPCs
source: Eleven out of the 53 genes tested exhibited consistent reduction in mRNA levels upon miR-128 overexpression in cultured mouse NPCs (Pcm1, Lmbr1l, Foxo4, Sh2d3c, Nfia, Pde8b, Sec24a, Pde3a, Fbxl20, Ypel3 and Kcnk10, Figure 4—source data 2, highlighted in yellow).
evidence: qPCR analysis shown in Figure 4—source data 2 identifies genes with consistent downregulation

claim: Only Pcm1, Nfia, Foxo4, and Fbxl20 were consistently upregulated upon miR-128 inhibition
source: The 11 genes were further tested for reciprocal upregulation when miR-128 was inhibited. qPCR analysis following miR-128 inhibition showed that only Pcm1, Nfia, Foxo4, and Fbxl20 were consistently upregulated among which Pcm1 displayed the greatest change (Figure 4—source data 3).
evidence: qPCR data shown in Figure 4—source data 3 demonstrates reciprocal upregulation upon miR-128 inhibition

claim: Co-transfection of miR-128 with the WT-Pcm1 reporter construct markedly suppressed luciferase activity by 58%
source: In this assay, co-transfection of miR-128 with the WT-Pcm1 reporter construct markedly suppressed the luciferase activity (by 58%, Figure 4B).
evidence: Luciferase reporter assay data in Figure 4B demonstrates direct targeting of Pcm1 3'-UTR by miR-128

claim: Mutating the seed sequences in the Pcm1 3'-UTR abolished miR-128-mediated suppression of PCM1 luciferase activity
source: Mutating these seed sequences abolished the miR-128-mediated suppression of PCM1 luciferase activity and restored the luciferase activity to the control level (Figure 4B), indicating the specificity of miR-128 targeting of the 3'-UTR of Pcm1.
evidence: Luciferase assay with mutant construct shown in Figure 4B demonstrates specificity of miR-128 targeting

claim: miR-128 overexpression significantly reduces PCM1 mRNA levels
source: We observed that miR-128 overexpression significantly reduced PCM1 mRNA (Figure 4C) and protein levels (Figure 4D).
evidence: qPCR data in Figure 4C demonstrates reduction in PCM1 mRNA upon miR-128 overexpression

claim: miR-128 overexpression significantly reduces PCM1 protein levels
source: We observed that miR-128 overexpression significantly reduced PCM1 mRNA (Figure 4C) and protein levels (Figure 4D).
evidence: Western blot analysis in Figure 4D demonstrates reduction in PCM1 protein upon miR-128 overexpression

claim: miR-128 knockdown increases PCM1 mRNA levels
source: Conversely, miR-128 knockdown using a specific inhibitor of miR-128 (anti-miR-128) (Smrt et al., 2010), in comparison to using a scrambled anti-miR (anti-miR-control) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) in NPCs produced the opposite effect on the expression of PCM1 mRNA (Figure 4E) and protein (Figure 4F).
evidence: qPCR data in Figure 4E demonstrates increased PCM1 mRNA upon miR-128 knockdown, with reference to Smrt et al., 2010

claim: miR-128 knockdown increases PCM1 protein levels
source: Conversely, miR-128 knockdown using a specific inhibitor of miR-128 (anti-miR-128) (Smrt et al., 2010), in comparison to using a scrambled anti-miR (anti-miR-control) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) in NPCs produced the opposite effect on the expression of PCM1 mRNA (Figure 4E) and protein (Figure 4F).
evidence: Western blot analysis in Figure 4F demonstrates increased PCM1 protein upon miR-128 knockdown, with reference to Smrt et al., 2010

claim: There is an inverse relationship between miR-128 and PCM1 mRNA levels in VZ/SVZ, IZ, and CP
source: In addition, qPCR analyses of tissue samples that were isolated from the VZ/SVZ, IZ, and CP using laser capture microdissection (LCM) (Wang et al., 2009) revealed an inverse relationship between miR-128 and PCM1 mRNA (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: qPCR data from laser capture microdissection samples shown in Figure 4G and H demonstrates inverse expression patterns, with reference to Wang et al., 2009

claim: miR-128 expression gradually increases from E12.5 through P0
source: An inverse relationship between miR-128 and PCM1 mRNA levels was also evident temporally, given that the expression of miR-128 gradually increased starting from E12.5 through P0, whereas PCM1 protein expression was found to gradually decrease over this time period (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–B), suggesting that miR-128 might regulate PCM1 levels to control NPC proliferation and differentiation in the developing cortex.
evidence: Temporal expression analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A demonstrates increasing miR-128 levels during development

claim: PCM1 protein expression gradually decreases from E12.5 through P0
source: An inverse relationship between miR-128 and PCM1 mRNA levels was also evident temporally, given that the expression of miR-128 gradually increased starting from E12.5 through P0, whereas PCM1 protein expression was found to gradually decrease over this time period (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–B), suggesting that miR-128 might regulate PCM1 levels to control NPC proliferation and differentiation in the developing cortex.
evidence: Western blot analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B demonstrates decreasing PCM1 protein levels during development, with inference about regulatory relationship

claim: PCM1 shRNA #2 leads to approximately 70% reduction in endogenous PCM1 in N2A cells
source: To test this hypothesis, we generated two small hairpin RNA (shRNA) vectors that expressed shRNAs that targeted mouse PCM1 and validated the efficiency of these shRNAs in knocking down PCM1 in mouse neuroblastoma (N2A) cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A). The expression of the shRNA vectors #1 and #2 led to a reduction in endogenous PCM1 of approximately 60 and 70%, respectively.
evidence: Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A quantifies the knockdown efficiency

claim: PCM1 knockdown leads to a 35% reduction in BrdU incorporation in NPCs
source: The reduction of endogenous PCM1 via shRNA led to significant inhibition of NPC proliferation, as indicated by a 35% reduction in BrdU incorporation by transfected cells compared with the BrdU incorporation by NPCs that were transfected with a control scrambled shRNA (Figure 5A and 5B); this reduction was comparable to that caused by the overexpression of miR-128 in NPCs (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: BrdU incorporation assay data in Figure 5A and 5B quantifies the reduction in proliferation upon PCM1 knockdown

claim: PCM1 knockdown does not affect cell survival
source: PCM1 knockdown did not affect cell survival, as indicated by TUNEL assay and antibody staining against activated caspase-3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: TUNEL and caspase-3 staining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 demonstrates no effect on apoptosis

claim: PCM1 shRNA expression significantly increases neuronal differentiation of NPCs by approximately 60%
source: Similar to miR-128 overexpression, PCM1 shRNA expression significantly increased the neuronal differentiation of NPCs (by approximately 60% compared with that of scrambled shRNA-transfected NPCs, Figure 5C and D).
evidence: TUJ1 immunostaining data in Figure 5C and D quantifies the increase in neuronal differentiation upon PCM1 knockdown

claim: PCM1 overexpression increases NPC proliferation by 70%
source: To examine whether PCM1 overexpression would exert the opposite effect of PCM1 knockdown in NPCs, we co-expressed PCM1 (without its 3'-UTR) in NPCs using a GFP expression construct and found that PCM1 overexpression increased the proliferation of NPCs compared to the vector-only control treatment (70% increase in BrdU and GFP double-positive cells) (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A and B).
evidence: BrdU incorporation assay data in Figure 5—figure supplement 4 quantifies the increase in proliferation upon PCM1 overexpression

claim: PCM1 overexpression decreases neurogenesis by 35% as determined by TUJ1 immunostaining
source: However, PCM1 overexpression decreased neurogenesis, as determined by immunostaining for TUJ1 (35% decrease in the number of TUJ1 and GFP double-positive cells) (Figure 5—figure supplement 5A and B) and MAP2 (45% decrease in the number of MAP2 and GFP double-positive cells) (Figure 5—figure supplement 5C and D).
evidence: TUJ1 immunostaining data in Figure 5—figure supplement 5A and B quantifies the decrease in neurogenesis

claim: PCM1 overexpression decreases neurogenesis by 45% as determined by MAP2 immunostaining
source: However, PCM1 overexpression decreased neurogenesis, as determined by immunostaining for TUJ1 (35% decrease in the number of TUJ1 and GFP double-positive cells) (Figure 5—figure supplement 5A and B) and MAP2 (45% decrease in the number of MAP2 and GFP double-positive cells) (Figure 5—figure supplement 5C and D).
evidence: MAP2 immunostaining data in Figure 5—figure supplement 5C and D quantifies the decrease in neurogenesis

claim: PCM1 overexpression has no effect on apoptosis
source: TUNEL and activated caspase-3 staining demonstrated that PCM1 overexpression had no effect on apoptosis (Figure 5—figure supplement 6).
evidence: TUNEL and caspase-3 staining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 6 demonstrates no effect on apoptosis

claim: PCM1 overexpression in vivo leads to a significant increase (20% ± SD) in the percentage of horizontally dividing cells
source: We observed a significant increase in the percentage of horizontally dividing cells upon PCM1 overexpression (Figure 5—figure supplement 7B, 20% ± SD).
evidence: Mitotic spindle orientation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 7B quantifies the change in division orientation

claim: PCM1 expression in vivo leads to a 40% increase in EdU and GFP double-positive cells
source: In addition, the expression of exogenous PCM1 in vivo led to a marked increase in the number of cells that incorporated EdU (40% increase in EdU and GFP double-positive cells) (Figure 5—figure supplement 7C and D).
evidence: EdU incorporation data in Figure 5—figure supplement 7C and D quantifies the increase in proliferation

claim: PCM1 overexpression in vivo leads to a 60% increase in PAX6 and GFP double-positive cells
source: Furthermore, we observed a marked increase in the number of PAX6-positive apical progenitor cells (60% increase in PAX6 and GFP double-positive cells) (Figure 5—figure supplement 7E and F) and a decrease in the number of TBR2-positive intermediate progenitor cells in brains in which NPCs had been electroporated with PCM1 (40% decrease in TBR2 and GFP double-positive cells) (Figure 5—figure supplement 7G and H).
evidence: PAX6 immunostaining data in Figure 5—figure supplement 7E and F quantifies the increase in apical progenitors

claim: PCM1 overexpression in vivo leads to a 40% decrease in TBR2 and GFP double-positive cells
source: Furthermore, we observed a marked increase in the number of PAX6-positive apical progenitor cells (60% increase in PAX6 and GFP double-positive cells) (Figure 5—figure supplement 7E and F) and a decrease in the number of TBR2-positive intermediate progenitor cells in brains in which NPCs had been electroporated with PCM1 (40% decrease in TBR2 and GFP double-positive cells) (Figure 5—figure supplement 7G and H).
evidence: TBR2 immunostaining data in Figure 5—figure supplement 7G and H quantifies the decrease in basal progenitors

claim: PCM1 overexpression in vivo leads to a 25% decrease in neuronal differentiation of NPCs
source: We monitored the neuronal differentiation of PCM1-expressing NPCs in vivo using NEUN staining and observed a 25% decrease in the neuronal differentiation of the NPCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 7I and J).
evidence: NEUN immunostaining data in Figure 5—figure supplement 7I and J quantifies the decrease in neurogenesis

claim: PCM1 overexpression rescues the decrease in NPC proliferation caused by miR-128 overexpression (103% versus 62% for BrdU and GFP double-positive cells)
source: We found that PCM1 overexpression rescued the decrease in NPC proliferation (103% versus 62% for BrdU and GFP double-positive cells, Figure 6A and B), and reversed the observed increase in neuronal differentiation induced by miR-128 overexpression (150% versus 225% for TUJ1 and GFP double-positive cells, Figure 6C and D; 115% versus 160% for MAP2 and GFP double-positive cells; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B) in vitro.
evidence: BrdU incorporation assay data in Figure 6A and B demonstrates rescue of proliferation phenotype

claim: PCM1 overexpression reverses the increase in neuronal differentiation induced by miR-128 overexpression (150% versus 225% for TUJ1 and GFP double-positive cells)
source: We found that PCM1 overexpression rescued the decrease in NPC proliferation (103% versus 62% for BrdU and GFP double-positive cells, Figure 6A and B), and reversed the observed increase in neuronal differentiation induced by miR-128 overexpression (150% versus 225% for TUJ1 and GFP double-positive cells, Figure 6C and D; 115% versus 160% for MAP2 and GFP double-positive cells; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B) in vitro.
evidence: TUJ1 immunostaining data in Figure 6C and D demonstrates rescue of neurogenesis phenotype

claim: Co-expression of PCM1 with miR-128 in vivo reverses the effects of miR-128 on neural stem cell proliferation (100% versus 75% for EdU and GFP double-positive cells)
source: To further verify these results in vivo, we co-electroporated the PCM1 expression vector with miR-128 in utero. Similarly, we found that co-expression of PCM1 with miR-128 successfully reversed the effects of miR-128 on neural stem cell proliferation (100% versus 75% for EdU and GFP double-positive cells, Figure 7A and B), PAX6 (78% versus 60% for PAX6 and GFP double-positive cells, Figure 7C and D), and TBR2 expression (120% versus 160% for TBR2 and GFP double-positive cells, Figure 7E and F) as well as on neuronal differentiation (100% versus 123% for NEUN-positive cells, Figure 7G and H).
evidence: EdU incorporation data in Figure 7A and B demonstrates rescue of proliferation phenotype in vivo

claim: Co-expression of PCM1 with miR-128 in vivo reverses the effects of miR-128 on PAX6 expression (78% versus 60% for PAX6 and GFP double-positive cells)
source: To further verify these results in vivo, we co-electroporated the PCM1 expression vector with miR-128 in utero. Similarly, we found that co-expression of PCM1 with miR-128 successfully reversed the effects of miR-128 on neural stem cell proliferation (100% versus 75% for EdU and GFP double-positive cells, Figure 7A and B), PAX6 (78% versus 60% for PAX6 and GFP double-positive cells, Figure 7C and D), and TBR2 expression (120% versus 160% for TBR2 and GFP double-positive cells, Figure 7E and F) as well as on neuronal differentiation (100% versus 123% for NEUN-positive cells, Figure 7G and H).
evidence: PAX6 immunostaining data in Figure 7C and D demonstrates rescue of apical progenitor phenotype in vivo

claim: Co-expression of PCM1 with miR-128 in vivo reverses the effects of miR-128 on TBR2 expression (120% versus 160% for TBR2 and GFP double-positive cells)
source: To further verify these results in vivo, we co-electroporated the PCM1 expression vector with miR-128 in utero. Similarly, we found that co-expression of PCM1 with miR-128 successfully reversed the effects of miR-128 on neural stem cell proliferation (100% versus 75% for EdU and GFP double-positive cells, Figure 7A and B), PAX6 (78% versus 60% for PAX6 and GFP double-positive cells, Figure 7C and D), and TBR2 expression (120% versus 160% for TBR2 and GFP double-positive cells, Figure 7E and F) as well as on neuronal differentiation (100% versus 123% for NEUN-positive cells, Figure 7G and H).
evidence: TBR2 immunostaining data in Figure 7E and F demonstrates rescue of basal progenitor phenotype in vivo

claim: Co-expression of PCM1 with miR-128 in vivo reverses the effects of miR-128 on neuronal differentiation (100% versus 123% for NEUN-positive cells)
source: To further verify these results in vivo, we co-electroporated the PCM1 expression vector with miR-128 in utero. Similarly, we found that co-expression of PCM1 with miR-128 successfully reversed the effects of miR-128 on neural stem cell proliferation (100% versus 75% for EdU and GFP double-positive cells, Figure 7A and B), PAX6 (78% versus 60% for PAX6 and GFP double-positive cells, Figure 7C and D), and TBR2 expression (120% versus 160% for TBR2 and GFP double-positive cells, Figure 7E and F) as well as on neuronal differentiation (100% versus 123% for NEUN-positive cells, Figure 7G and H).
evidence: NEUN immunostaining data in Figure 7G and H demonstrates rescue of neurogenesis phenotype in vivo

claim: miR-128 regulates the proliferation and differentiation of NPCs in the murine embryonic cortex by targeting PCM1 expression through a direct interaction with its 3'UTR
source: Taken together, these results strongly suggest that miR-128 regulates the proliferation and differentiation of NPCs in the murine embryonic cortex by targeting PCM1 expression though a direct interaction with its 3'UTR.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the collective experimental evidence from luciferase assays, rescue experiments, and phenotypic analyses

claim: miR-128 has previously been shown to play a crucial role in cortical migration
source: In this study, we demonstrate that miR-128, which has previously been shown to play a crucial role in cortical migration (Franzoni et al., 2015), inhibits self-renewal and promotes neuronal differentiation in mouse NPCs by targeting pericentriolar material 1 (PCM1), a critical protein for cell division, during early cortical development (Ge et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Franzoni et al., 2015

claim: PCM1 is a critical protein for cell division during early cortical development
source: In this study, we demonstrate that miR-128, which has previously been shown to play a crucial role in cortical migration (Franzoni et al., 2015), inhibits self-renewal and promotes neuronal differentiation in mouse NPCs by targeting pericentriolar material 1 (PCM1), a critical protein for cell division, during early cortical development (Ge et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ge et al., 2010

claim: Neurogenesis involves the proliferation and neuronal fate specification of NPCs and the subsequent maturation and functional integration of the neuronal progeny into neuronal circuits
source: Neurogenesis, the process by which functionally integrated neurons are generated from neural progenitor cells (NPCs), involves the proliferation and neuronal fate specification of NPCs and the subsequent maturation and functional integration of the neuronal progeny into neuronal circuits (Gupta et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gupta et al., 2002

claim: Disruption of neurogenesis has been associated with autism spectrum disorders, Treacher Collins syndrome, and various neural tube defects
source: Given its importance in the development of the nervous system, neurogenesis is tightly regulated at many levels by both extrinsic and intrinsic factors (Heng et al., 2010), and its disruption has been associated with various pathologies, including autism spectrum disorders (ASDs), Treacher Collins syndrome, and various neural tube defects (Sun and Hevner, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Heng et al., 2010 and Sun and Hevner, 2014

claim: miRNAs function through imperfect base-pairing with complementary sequences in target mRNA molecules, typically triggering their targeted degradation or translational repression by RISC
source: Encoded by eukaryotic nuclear DNA, miRNAs function through imperfect base-pairing with complementary sequences in target mRNA molecules, typically triggering their targeted degradation or translational repression by the RNA-induced silencing complex RISC (Bartel, 2009; Shi et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bartel, 2009 and Shi et al., 2010

claim: The specific spatiotemporal expression of miRNAs may be essential for brain morphogenesis and neurogenesis
source: The role of miRNAs in neuronal development and function has recently received increased attention, and the specific spatiotemporal expression of these molecules may be essential for brain morphogenesis and neurogenesis (Volvert et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Volvert et al., 2012 and Zhang et al., 2014

claim: Twenty-eight miRNAs were expressed at significantly different levels in ASD brains compared with non-autism control brains
source: Abu-Elneel et al. investigated the expression of 466 human miRNAs from postmortem cerebellar cortical tissue from individuals with ASDs and identified twenty-eight miRNAs that were expressed at significantly different levels in the ASD brains compared with the non-autism control brains (Abu-Elneel et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Abu-Elneel et al., 2008

claim: Only three miRNAs (miR-7, miR-128, and miR-132) among the dysregulated miRNAs in ASD brains were exclusively expressed in the brain
source: Interestingly, of these dysegulated miRNAs, only three of them (miR-7, miR-128, and miR-132) were exclusively expressed in the brain (Li and Jin, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Li and Jin, 2010

claim: miR-128 is transcribed from two distinct loci, miR-128-1 and miR-128-2, as two primary transcripts that are processed into identical mature miRNA sequences
source: miR-128 is transcribed from two distinct loci, miR-128-1 and miR-128-2, as two primary transcripts that are processed into identical mature miRNA sequences (Adlakha and Saini, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Adlakha and Saini, 2014

claim: Downregulation of miR-128 has been reported in glioblastoma and medulloblastoma
source: Previously, downregulation of miR-128 has been reported in several brain cancers, including glioblastoma and medulloblastoma (Adlakha and Saini, 2013; Peruzzi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Adlakha and Saini, 2013 and Peruzzi et al., 2013

claim: Allelic loss of chromosome 3p, where miRNA-128-2 is encoded, has been associated with the most aggressive forms of neuroblastoma
source: Consistent with these findings, allelic loss of chromosome 3p, where miRNA-128-2 is encoded, has also been associated with the most aggressive forms of neuroblastoma, indicating that miR-128 may play an important role in the cell cycle as well as growth and differentiation (Adlakha and Saini, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Adlakha and Saini, 2014, with inference about miR-128's role

claim: Loss of PCM1 triggers NPCs to exit the cell cycle early and promotes premature differentiation of NPCs to neurons
source: The observed effects of miR-128 are consistent with a previous study by Ge et al. that demonstrated that the loss of PCM1 triggered NPCs to exit the cell cycle early and promoted the premature differentiation of NPCs to neurons (Ge et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ge et al., 2010

claim: Knockdown of PCM1 results in impaired interkinetic nuclear migration of NPCs, leading to overproduction of neurons and premature depletion of the NPC pool
source: In this study, knockdown of PCM1 resulted in impaired interkinetic nuclear migration of NPCs, which leads to the overproduction of neurons and to premature depletion of the NPC pool in the developing neocortex.
evidence: This claim refers to findings from Ge et al., 2010 as discussed in the manuscript

claim: Nine novel missense mutations in the Pcm1 gene have been identified in ASD patients
source: Intriguingly, we recently identified 9 novel (i.e., previously unreported) missense mutations in the Pcm1 gene in ASD patients (H.S.J. and S.G.R., unpublished observations), indicating that PCM1 misregulation might be a core mechanism in some ASD patients with disrupted cortical development.
evidence: This claim is based on unpublished observations by the authors

claim: Reduced miR-128 expression triggers early onset of hyperactivity, seizures, and death in miR-128-2 knockout mice
source: By selectively inactivating miR-128-2 in forebrain neurons using Camk2a-Cre and floxed miR-128-2, Tan et al. found that reduced miR-128 expression triggered the early onset of hyperactivity, seizures, and death (Tan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tan et al., 2013

claim: miR-128 may regulate the expression of numerous ion channels and transporters as well as genes that contribute to neurotransmitter-driven neuronal excitability and motor activity
source: Based on their bioinformatics network and pathway analyses of miR-128 target genes, those authors found that miR-128 may regulate the expression of numerous ion channels and transporters as well as genes that contribute to neurotransmitter-driven neuronal excitability and motor activity (Tan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tan et al., 2013

claim: NPCs are not excitable due to a lack of active sodium channels
source: Because NPCs are not excitable due to a lack of active sodium channels (Li et al., 2008), it is unlikely that the cellular effects of miR-128 observed here resulted from changes in the expression of ion channels or transporters.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2008, with inference about the mechanism

claim: During development, NPCs in the VZ maintain proliferative capacity and the ability to self-renew (apical progenitors, APs)
source: During development, NPCs in the VZ maintain proliferative capacity and the ability to self-renew (apical progenitors, APs). These APs give rise to intermediate progenitors (basal progenitors, BPs) within the SVZ and IZ that can proliferate and become neurons (Martinez-Cerdeno et al., 2006; Pontious et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Martinez-Cerdeno et al., 2006 and Pontious et al., 2008

claim: Apical progenitors give rise to intermediate progenitors (basal progenitors, BPs) within the SVZ and IZ that can proliferate and become neurons
source: During development, NPCs in the VZ maintain proliferative capacity and the ability to self-renew (apical progenitors, APs). These APs give rise to intermediate progenitors (basal progenitors, BPs) within the SVZ and IZ that can proliferate and become neurons (Martinez-Cerdeno et al., 2006; Pontious et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Martinez-Cerdeno et al., 2006 and Pontious et al., 2008

claim: Basal progenitors will generate the bulk of cortical neurons
source: Because BPs will generate the bulk of cortical neurons (Tan and Shi, 2013), we tested whether miR-128 regulates the neuronal differentiation of NPCs in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tan and Shi, 2013

claim: miR-128 acts on two different stages of NPC development: first, by regulating symmetric/asymmetric division of APs to promote BP production; and second, by enhancing the exit of BPs from the cell cycle to promote overall neurogenesis
source: Taken together, these results indicate that miR-128 may act on two different stages of NPC development: first, by regulating symmetric/asymmetric division of APs, miR-128 promotes BP production; and second, by enhancing the exit of BPs from the cell cycle, miR-128 promotes overall neurogenesis (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the collective experimental data from in vivo experiments, with a schematic shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: Downregulation of miR-128 in early neuronal precursors impedes their developmental progression by causing them to be retained in a more primitive, proliferative stage
source: In contrast, downregulation of miR-128 in early neuronal precursors impeded their developmental progression by causing them to be retained in a more primitive, proliferative stage, resulting in the expansion of a pool of the NPC pool.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations of miR-128 knockdown effects

claim: The cerebral cortex is responsible for cognitive, motor and perceptual behaviors
source: The cerebral cortex, which is the most complex structure of the brain, is responsible for cognitive, motor and perceptual behaviors (Volvert et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Volvert et al., 2012

claim: The generation of cortical neurons depends on NPCs exiting the cell cycle, migrating, and subsequently partially maturing into neurons
source: The generation of cortical neurons depends on NPCs exiting the cell cycle, migrating, and subsequently partially maturing into neurons. These processes are orchestrated by multiple gene products that ultimately converge on the cytoskeleton to support morphological remodeling (Sun and Hevner, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sun and Hevner, 2014

claim: Lack of regulation of neurogenesis may result in cortical malformations associated with certain neuropsychiatric disorders
source: Therefore, for all of these processes to be correctly executed, the timing and abundance of specific gene products must be precisely regulated, and a lack of regulation may result in the cortical malformations that are associated with certain neuropsychiatric disorders (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2014

claim: miRNAs are abundant, short-lived double-stranded RNAs of ~20-25 nucleotides derived from endogenous short-hairpin transcripts
source: miRNAs are abundant, short-lived double-stranded RNAs of ~20-25 nucleotides that are derived from endogenous short-hairpin transcripts (Bartel, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bartel, 2009

claim: miRNAs introduce an additional level of intricacy to gene regulation in neurogenesis
source: miRNAs contribute to various developmental processes by acting as post-transcriptional regulators; thus, they introduce an additional level of intricacy to gene regulation in neurogenesis.
evidence: This is a general statement about miRNA function based on established knowledge

claim: miRNAs play a primary role in fine-tuning signaling pathways that control the synchronized steps of cortical development
source: Recent data obtained by several groups support a primary role of miRNAs in fine-tuning signaling pathways that control the synchronized steps of cortical development (Kawahara et al., 2012; Shi et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kawahara et al., 2012 and Shi et al., 2010

claim: Aberrant miR-128 expression may account for abnormal cortical development underlying the pathophysiology of certain neuropsychiatric disorders, including autism
source: Taken together, our data indicate that miR-128 is an important regulator of neurogenesis in the embryonic cortex and suggest that aberrant miR-128 expression may account for the abnormal cortical development that underlies the pathophysiology of certain neuropsychiatric disorders, including autism.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the experimental findings and their potential clinical implications
